prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

While the members of the Type IIn category of supernovae are united by the presence of strong multicomponent Balmer emission lines in their spectra, they are quite heterogeneous with respect to other properties such as Balmer line profiles, light curves, strength of radio emission, and intrinsic brightness. We are now beginning to see variety among SNe IIn in their polarimetric characteristics as well, some but not all of which may be due to inclination angle effects. The increasing number of known "hybrid" SNe with IIn-like emission lines suggests that circumstellar material may be more common around all types of SNe than previously thought. Investigation of the correlations between spectropolarimetric signatures and other IIn attributes will help us address the question of classification of "interacting SNe" and the possibility of distinguishing different groups within the diverse IIn subclass.

Type IIn supernovae are defined by their strong, multicomponent Balmer emission lines, which arise from interactions between the supernova ejecta and surrounding circumstellar material. Beyond this shared feature, however, they exhibit substantial diversity. Individual events differ in their Balmer-line profiles, light-curve shapes and evolution, radio-emission strength, intrinsic luminosity, and polarimetric properties.

At least some of the observed polarimetric variation may reflect differences in viewing angle rather than fundamental differences in the explosions themselves. If the circumstellar material or ejecta are distributed asymmetrically, the measured polarization can change considerably depending on the observer’s line of sight.

The increasing discovery of hybrid supernovae that display IIn-like emission alongside characteristics of other spectroscopic classes also suggests that dense circumstellar material may be common around many types of supernova progenitors. Systematic studies of the relationships between spectropolarimetric signatures and other observational properties could therefore improve the classification of interacting supernovae. Such correlations may also reveal physically distinct groups within the diverse Type IIn subclass.
outputs.L4:
Type IIn supernovae are defined observationally by narrow hydrogen emission lines produced when rapidly expanding supernova ejecta interact with slower, hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM). Despite this common spectroscopic feature, the class is remarkably heterogeneous. Individual events display wide variations in line profiles and evolution, optical luminosity and light-curve shape, radio and X-ray emission, and inferred mass-loss histories. Their brightness can range from that of relatively modest explosions to that of the most luminous supernovae known. Polarimetric properties are similarly diverse, indicating substantial differences in the geometry and distribution of both the ejecta and the surrounding material.

Spectropolarimetry offers a particularly valuable way to investigate this diversity because it provides information about geometry that cannot be recovered from total-flux spectra alone. Continuum polarization may reveal large-scale asymmetry in the ejecta or in the interaction region, while changes in polarization across emission lines can distinguish among contributions from the photosphere, shocked gas, and unshocked CSM. The evolution of these signatures can also show how the effective emitting region changes as the shock propagates outward. By comparing spectropolarimetric observations with light-curve morphology, luminosity, spectral-line properties, radio and X-ray behavior, and estimates of CSM density, researchers can test whether apparently different Type IIn events arise from distinct physical systems or from variations within a continuous population.

Inclination effects must be considered in such comparisons. If the circumstellar environment is disk-like, toroidal, bipolar, clumpy, or otherwise nonspherical, the observed properties can depend strongly on viewing angle. An equatorial concentration of dense material viewed edge-on may produce prominent narrow lines, strong obscuration, and a large polarization signal, whereas the same structure viewed closer to its symmetry axis could appear less polarized and may display different line profiles or luminosity evolution. Some of the diversity assigned to intrinsic differences in progenitors or explosion energies may therefore result from orientation. Coordinated modeling of spectra, polarization, and multiwavelength emission is needed to separate geometric effects from genuine differences in CSM mass, composition, radial extent, and density.

The importance of this issue extends beyond the traditional Type IIn category. A growing number of hybrid or transitional supernovae show evidence for interaction only during particular phases of their evolution. Some initially resemble ordinary hydrogen-rich or stripped-envelope explosions and later develop narrow emission lines when their ejecta encounter a detached shell. Others show signatures of interaction with hydrogen-poor material or exhibit characteristics associated with more than one spectroscopic class. These events suggest that dense, structured CSM is not restricted to the progenitors of Type IIn supernovae. Instead, enhanced mass loss shortly before explosion may occur across a broad range of massive-star systems, possibly through eruptive activity, binary interaction, envelope stripping, or instabilities during late nuclear burning.

Systematic correlations among polarization, spectroscopy, photometry, radio and X-ray emission, and host-environment properties could therefore lead to a more physically meaningful classification of interacting supernovae. Such studies may identify subgroups within the Type IIn class associated with different CSM geometries, mass-loss mechanisms, progenitor systems, or interaction timescales. They may also clarify which hybrid events are fundamentally related to Type IIn explosions and which merely pass through a similar observational phase. Ultimately, incorporating geometry and viewing angle into classification schemes should help transform the Type IIn label from a broad phenomenological category into a framework that more directly reflects the physical origins and circumstellar environments of interacting supernovae.
outputs.L5: In programming, a **While** loop repeats a block of code as long as a specified condition remains true. The **Type** of data used within the loop—such as an integer, string, or Boolean—determines which operations can be performed. A name like **IIn** may represent a custom interface, input component, or identifier, depending on the language and project. Together, While, Type, and IIn can form part of a structured program that processes input safely and efficiently.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the diversity of Type IIn supernovae, focusing on their spectral, photometric, radio, and polarimetric properties.
counterfactuals.output:
Type IIn supernovae are defined observationally by relatively narrow hydrogen emission lines produced when fast supernova ejecta interact with dense, hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM). They are not a uniform explosion class: similar signatures can arise from different progenitors, mass-loss histories, CSM geometries, and even thermonuclear explosions embedded in hydrogen-rich material.

### Spectral diversity
- Their characteristic Hα profiles often combine:
  - **Narrow components**—typically tens to a few hundred km s⁻¹—from unshocked, photoionized CSM.
  - **Intermediate-width components**—roughly \(10^3\)–\(10^4\) km s⁻¹—from shocked gas or a cool dense shell.
  - **Broad wings**, sometimes extending to many thousands of km s⁻¹, produced by fast ejecta and/or electron scattering in optically thick CSM.
- Line profiles range from symmetric Lorentzian shapes to multi-peaked or asymmetric profiles, indicating large differences in optical depth and CSM geometry.
- Ionization conditions vary widely. Some objects show strong He lines, Fe-group emission, or high-ionization “coronal” lines, while others remain dominated by Balmer emission.
- Spectral evolution ranges from persistent interaction signatures lasting years to narrow lines that disappear quickly as confined CSM is swept up.
- Late-time blueshifted or asymmetric lines may signal newly formed dust, occultation in an optically thick shell, or intrinsically asymmetric interaction.
- Rare “Ia-CSM” events demonstrate that an underlying thermonuclear explosion can mimic the Type IIn interaction spectrum.

### Photometric diversity
- Peak luminosities span ordinary core-collapse values to the superluminous regime. In the brightest events, kinetic energy is efficiently converted into radiation through CSM interaction.
- Rise times range from days to many weeks, reflecting differences in CSM radius, density, and diffusion time.
- Light curves may be:
  - Rapidly declining,
  - Slowly fading for months or years,
  - Approximately linear,
  - Plateau-like, as in the **IIn-P** group,
  - Irregular or rebrightening because the shock encounters shells or density enhancements.
- Some show precursor eruptions months to years before explosion, suggesting episodic, LBV-like mass loss, although precursors are not universal.
- Their colors and inferred temperatures are likewise varied, and substantial host or circumstellar extinction can obscure the true luminosity.
- Long-lived luminosity often tracks continued shock interaction rather than radioactive \(^{56}\)Co decay, although radioactive heating may also contribute.

### Radio properties
- Radio emission is synchrotron radiation from shock-accelerated electrons in amplified magnetic fields.
- Radio luminosities and turn-on times vary enormously. Some Type IIn events become exceptionally bright radio sources and remain detectable for years or decades; others are weak or undetected.
- Dense ionized CSM can delay or suppress radio emission through free–free absorption, while synchrotron self-absorption may also matter.
- Late radio emergence can occur only after the shock reaches less opaque material. Conversely, bumps and changes in the radio light curve reveal clumpy CSM, shells, or abrupt changes in the progenitor’s mass-loss rate.
- Thus, an optical classification as Type IIn does not guarantee strong early radio emission.

### Polarimetric properties
- Many Type IIn supernovae show appreciable intrinsic continuum polarization, often around the percent level and occasionally higher, implying a globally aspherical photosphere or CSM.
- Polarization commonly varies across Hα and other lines. Line depolarization, loops in the Stokes \(Q\)-\(U\) plane, and changing polarization angles indicate that the line-emitting region, electron-scattering region, and obscuring material have different geometries.
- Time evolution can reveal inner structures as the effective photosphere recedes, or changes as the shock overtakes an equatorial disk, torus, bipolar outflow, or clumpy wind.
- Some objects show low polarization, so strong asphericity is common but not universal; viewing angle can also hide an intrinsically nonspherical configuration.

Overall, Type IIn diversity is best understood as diversity in **interaction conditions** rather than a single progenitor channel. Variations in CSM density, radial extent, composition, clumping, and geometry—combined with differences in explosion type and viewing angle—produce the broad range of spectra, light curves, radio behavior, and polarization.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise academic paragraph explaining why SNe IIn are considered a heterogeneous supernova subclass and how spectropolarimetry may improve their classification.
counterfactuals.output: Type IIn supernovae (SNe IIn) are considered a heterogeneous subclass because their defining narrow hydrogen emission lines primarily indicate strong interaction with dense circumstellar material rather than a single progenitor or explosion mechanism. The class may therefore include explosions of diverse massive stars, thermonuclear events embedded in hydrogen-rich environments, and even non-terminal stellar eruptions, with substantial variation in circumstellar density, geometry, and temporal evolution. Spectropolarimetry can refine this phenomenological classification by revealing unresolved asymmetries in the ejecta and circumstellar medium: continuum polarization probes global geometry, while polarization changes across spectral lines distinguish differently distributed emitting and scattering regions. Such measurements can identify geometric and physical subgroups that appear similar in total-flux spectra, thereby linking SNe IIn more reliably to their progenitor systems and explosion channels.

counterfactuals.prompt: Discuss the defining characteristics of Type IIn supernovae, the role of circumstellar interaction, and the significance of “hybrid” interacting supernovae.
counterfactuals.output:
### Type IIn supernovae: defining characteristics

Type IIn supernovae are a spectroscopic subclass of hydrogen-rich core-collapse supernovae. The “n” denotes **narrow emission lines**, especially narrow Balmer lines such as Hα, superposed on broader emission components. Their characteristic spectra often contain:

- **Narrow lines**—typically tens to a few hundred km s⁻¹—from slowly moving, photoionized circumstellar material (CSM) expelled before explosion.
- **Intermediate-width components**—roughly \(10^3\)–\(10^4\) km s⁻¹—from shocked gas or electron-scattering effects.
- **Broad wings**, sometimes with Lorentzian profiles, produced by electron scattering in optically thick CSM and/or fast supernova ejecta.
- Blue, nearly featureless continua at early times when the interaction region is hot and optically thick.

Type IIn events are highly diverse. Some are extremely luminous and remain interaction-powered for years, while others show narrow lines only briefly. Their light curves can decline smoothly, display plateaus or multiple peaks, or show late-time rebrightening. Thus, “Type IIn” describes the observational importance of interaction with hydrogen-rich material rather than a single progenitor or explosion mechanism.

### Role of circumstellar interaction

The defining phenomenon is the collision of fast ejecta—moving at several thousand to tens of thousands of km s⁻¹—with dense, slower CSM. This collision creates:

1. A **forward shock** propagating into the CSM.
2. A **reverse shock** moving back into the expanding ejecta.
3. A dense, shocked region between them, which can cool efficiently and radiate strongly.

If the CSM density is high, a substantial fraction of the ejecta’s kinetic energy is converted into optical, ultraviolet, infrared, and X-ray radiation. Interaction can therefore make an otherwise ordinary explosion unusually luminous and can dominate or conceal the underlying supernova spectrum.

The CSM records the progenitor’s mass-loss history. Narrow-line velocities, luminosity evolution, and inferred density structure can reveal:

- Extreme pre-supernova mass-loss rates.
- Episodic eruptions or shells rather than steady winds.
- Asymmetric disks or clumpy material.
- The timing of mass loss, often years to decades before collapse.

Luminous blue variables are frequently invoked as progenitors because of their eruptive mass loss, but red supergiants, yellow hypergiants, binary-stripped stars, and other systems may also produce suitable CSM. Binary interaction may be especially important. Dense dust can form in the cooled shocked region, causing infrared emission and asymmetric optical-line profiles.

### “Hybrid” interacting supernovae

Hybrid events combine properties of more than one traditional class or change classification as different layers become visible. Examples include:

- Supernovae that initially resemble ordinary Type II-P or II-L events but later develop strong Type IIn interaction.
- Events with early narrow hydrogen lines that disappear once a confined CSM shell is swept up.
- Objects transitioning between hydrogen-rich Type IIn and helium-dominated Type Ibn behavior.
- **Ia-CSM** events, in which a likely thermonuclear Type Ia explosion interacts with hydrogen-rich CSM and consequently resembles a Type IIn.
- Supernovae whose interaction signatures appear only after the ejecta reach a distant shell, producing delayed rebrightening.

These hybrids are significant because they show that spectral classifications do not map uniquely onto explosion physics. Narrow hydrogen emission establishes interaction with hydrogen-rich material, but it does not by itself prove that the underlying explosion was a particular kind of core collapse. Hybrid events also reveal that CSM is often radially stratified, asymmetric, or episodic, preserving a time-resolved record of the progenitor’s final evolution.

More broadly, they connect otherwise separate supernova categories and emphasize the need for early discovery, repeated spectroscopy, multiwavelength monitoring, and late-time observations. A single spectrum may classify the transient’s current interaction state rather than identify its underlying progenitor or explosion mechanism.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: How can variations in polarization and viewing angle help astronomers distinguish different groups within the Type IIn supernova category?
counterfactuals.output:
Type IIn supernovae are identified by narrow hydrogen emission lines produced when fast ejecta interact with dense circumstellar material (CSM). Polarization adds geometric information that ordinary spectra cannot provide.

- **Continuum polarization** traces the overall asymmetry of the photosphere and/or electron-scattering CSM. High polarization generally indicates a strongly nonspherical structure—such as a disk, torus, or bipolar outflow—whereas low polarization may indicate a nearly spherical event or an asymmetric event viewed close to its symmetry axis.
- **Viewing-angle effects** can therefore make similar explosions look different. A dense equatorial CSM disk viewed edge-on may produce strong narrow-line interaction, extinction, and high polarization; the same system viewed pole-on may show weaker polarization and a different balance of narrow, intermediate, and broad emission components.
- **Polarization across spectral lines** separates emitting regions. Depolarization across narrow or intermediate-width Hα often means that relatively unpolarized line photons are diluting polarized continuum light. Peaks, loops, or rotations of the polarization angle across a line reveal clumps or misaligned ejecta and CSM.
- **Polarization angle and its evolution** test whether the geometry has a single stable axis. A constant angle suggests axisymmetric CSM, while angle changes with wavelength or time imply multiple structures—for example, asymmetric ejecta interacting with a differently oriented CSM disk.
- **Time-dependent measurements** probe different depths. As the shock expands and optical depth falls, changes in polarization can distinguish long-lived interaction with an extended CSM shell from interaction confined to a compact, highly asymmetric region.

Combining these signatures can divide Type IIn events into groups dominated by roughly spherical dense winds, disk- or torus-like CSM, clumpy or multi-axis environments, and cases whose apparent differences are mainly due to orientation. However, low polarization alone does not prove spherical symmetry, because an asymmetric explosion viewed along its axis can also appear nearly unpolarized.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-style conclusion about the diversity of SNe IIn and the value of correlating their spectropolarimetric signatures with Balmer-line profiles, light curves, radio emission, and intrinsic brightness.
counterfactuals.output:
## Conclusion

The observed diversity of Type IIn supernovae reflects substantial variation in progenitor mass-loss histories, circumstellar-medium structure, explosion properties, and viewing geometry. Spectropolarimetry provides a uniquely sensitive probe of this complexity by revealing departures from spherical symmetry that are unresolved in direct observations. Continuum polarization traces the global geometry of the photosphere and interaction region, while polarization changes across Balmer lines can distinguish among differently shaped or spatially separated emitting, absorbing, and scattering components.

The physical interpretation of these signatures is strongest when polarization is analyzed alongside Balmer-line profiles, optical light curves, radio emission, and intrinsic luminosity. Line widths, asymmetries, and temporal evolution constrain the kinematics and distribution of the hydrogen-rich circumstellar material; light-curve morphology and brightness measure the efficiency and duration of shock-powered radiation; and radio observations probe the density, extent, and clumpiness of the outer environment, subject to absorption effects. Correlations among these observables can therefore test whether highly luminous or slowly evolving events preferentially arise from dense, globally asymmetric circumstellar structures, whether multi-component Balmer profiles correspond to distinct polarization geometries, and whether radio-bright systems represent different mass-loss configurations from optically similar but radio-faint events.

No single observable is sufficient to separate intrinsic explosion asymmetry from circumstellar interaction and orientation effects. A coordinated, time-resolved, multiwavelength approach is thus essential for converting the phenomenological IIn designation into a more physically meaningful framework. Larger and less selection-biased spectropolarimetric samples, coupled with consistent measurements of line morphology, luminosity, light-curve evolution, and radio properties, should reveal whether SNe IIn form continuous distributions in geometry and circumstellar density or comprise several distinct progenitor and mass-loss channels. Such correlations offer one of the most direct routes to reconstructing the final stages of massive-star evolution and understanding the mechanisms responsible for extreme pre-supernova mass loss.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
